Right. It was my second week in Albania. We were supposed to reach Theth by six, but at four o'clock we were still climbing, and the rain was coming in sideways.
Good, that is enough scene. Now please do not ramble about the bike. What happened next?
I was about to turn back. Honestly, I had already turned the bike around. And then, out of the blue, a shepherd came down the path with a mule.

Hi Marcelo, it is Ingrid, from the ferry to Bergen. I have a favor to ask. I am recording a new episode of Saddle Stories next Thursday. I was going to interview a mountain guide, but he cancelled this morning. So I thought of you, and the story about the Albanian pass. You told it at dinner, and the whole table was hanging on your every word. Here is my only advice. Set the scene in two sentences, no more. Do not ramble about the bike or the gear. Get to the point, and keep the listeners in suspense until the shepherd appears. And please, do not cut a long story short at the end, because the ending is the best part. The episode is supposed to be twenty minutes, so you have about six. Call me tonight if you can. I would love to have you on the show.

Welcome back. Today, one simple question. Why do some travel stories work, and others die at the dinner table? Here is my answer. A good story is not about what happened. It is about what was supposed to happen. Every great anecdote starts with a plan. We were going to cross the mountains. I was supposed to be home by Sunday. The listener hears that plan and immediately starts waiting for it to go wrong. That waiting is suspense, and it is free. You do not need to embellish anything. The second trick is the near miss. I was about to give up. I was about to get on the wrong train. Those words make people lean forward. And the third trick is restraint. Set the scene quickly, cut the details nobody needs, and when you reach the twist, stop talking for one second. Most bad storytellers ramble because they are afraid of silence. The good ones use it.

First, Marcelo sets the scene: his second week in Albania, climbing toward Theth in the rain. Then he explains the plan: they were supposed to reach the village by six. After that, he admits he was about to turn back and had already turned the bike around. Next, out of the blue, a shepherd comes down the path with a mule, and Marcelo pauses to keep everyone in suspense. Finally, he delivers the punchline: the shepherd walks them over the pass and refuses to take any money.
